cues.text: A Sickly Child, a Franciscan Vow
Born Giovanni di Fidanza around 1221 near Bagnoregio in central Italy, the future Bonaventure survived a dangerous childhood illness, by his own later account.
His mother's fervent prayers and a vow made to St. Francis of Assisi, still alive at the time, were credited with his recovery.
This providential brush with death, whatever its precise historical details, left a lasting mark on the boy who would grow up to join the very order Francis had founded.
Studying Alongside Aquinas

Bonaventure entered the Franciscan order and was sent to complete his studies at the University of Paris , then the intellectual center of Christian Europe, studying under Alexander of Hales, the great founder of the Franciscan theological school.
There Bonaventure's path crossed repeatedly with that of a young Dominican friar of comparable brilliance, Thomas Aquinas .
The two men earned their teaching licenses together in 1257 and remained throughout their careers intellectual rivals in different theological emphases and genuine personal friends.
The whole Church has long treasured this friendship as a symbol of how two great minds, formed in different traditions, could pursue the same single truth without rancor.
Minister General in a Time of Crisis
In 1257, at only about thirty-six, Bonaventure was elected Minister General of the entire Franciscan order.
He inherited a movement that had grown, within a few decades of Francis's death, from barefoot companions into a vast international institution numbering many thousands of friars.
This scale of growth had opened bitter internal division over how literally the order's founding vow of absolute poverty should still be observed.
Bonaventure navigated this crisis with a characteristic blend of firmness and moderation.
He worked to hold together the order’s more rigorist and moderate factions without abandoning Francis's original vision.
At the request of his fellow friars, he composed a new official biography of Francis, presenting a single, unifying account of the founder's life and intentions for the whole order to follow.
The Seraphic Doctor
Bonaventure's theological writings were composed alongside his demanding administrative duties.
They combined rigorous Scholastic argument with a warmth and mystical intensity that distinguished his work from some contemporaries' more purely philosophical style.

His Itinerarium Mentis in Deum ("The Journey of the Mind to God") traces the soul's ascent toward God through successive stages of contemplation, ending in a mystical union beyond the reach of reason alone.
This fusion of careful theological argument with genuine, burning love for God earned Bonaventure, from later generations, the title Seraphic Doctor .
The name evokes the seraphim, the highest choir of angels, whose essential nature is pure, unmediated love of God.
A Council, and a Sudden Death
In 1273, Pope Gregory X made Bonaventure a cardinal and Bishop of Albano.
He called on him to help lead the Second Council of Lyon , convened with the ambitious hope of healing the long schism between the Eastern and Western Churches.
Bonaventure preached a sermon celebrating the brief, hard-won reunion the council achieved.

He died suddenly and unexpectedly only two days before the council's close—his own secretary's chronicle suggesting, though later scholarship has treated the claim cautiously, that he may have been poisoned.
Legacy
Bonaventure was buried the very evening of his death, honored with a splendid funeral attended by the pope himself and the assembled council fathers.
Canonized in 1482 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1588, Bonaventure remains, alongside his friend Aquinas, one of the two supreme theological minds of the thirteenth century.
This proves that the most rigorous intellectual argument and the most ardent mystical love of God were never, for Bonaventure, two separate pursuits.
Instead, they formed a single unbroken journey of the mind toward the God who had first called it into being.
